Sample text:
---
There is a specific kind of quiet magic in buying a secondhand book and realizing you aren’t the first person to have lived inside it.

Sometimes the evidence is subtle: a spine creased open to a particular chapter, as if the book itself remembers where it was left face-down on a nightstand. Other times, it is unmistakable. A name written on the inside cover in slanted cursive—*Eleanor, October 1974*—followed by a city she may no longer live in, or a version of herself she eventually outgrew.

The best discoveries, though, are in the margins.

Marginalia is an accidental time capsule. Unlike a diary, which is written with the self-conscious awareness of an audience—even if that audience is only a future self—notes in a book are impulsive. They are the raw sparks of a mind colliding with another mind on the page. 

You flip through a battered paperback of a nineteenth-century novel and find a single sentence double-underlined in faded blue ink, with a jagged *YES!* in the margin. You read the sentence, and suddenly you know something intimate about a stranger. You know what made them feel seen on an ordinary Tuesday thirty years ago. Three chapters later, there is a furious question mark pressed so hard into the paper it nearly tears through, or a penciled *nonsense* next to a philosopher’s grand claim. Even the mundane artifacts tell stories: a dried four-leaf clover pressed flat and brittle between pages 112 and 113; a boarding pass from a flight to Chicago used as a bookmark and forgotten; a phone number scribbled on the back flyleaf with no name attached, belonging to someone the reader was once certain they would never forget.

Reading a marked-up book turns a solitary act into a quiet conversation across time. You are no longer just listening to the author; you are sitting next to someone who listened before you, leaning over their shoulder to see what caught their eye. Sometimes you disagree with them. You wonder why they ignored a passage that stopped you cold, and why they bracketed a paragraph that seems completely ordinary to you. It is a gentle reminder that no two people ever actually read the exact same book. We each bring our own weather to the page.

There is something increasingly rare about this in an age of glass screens and cloud-synced libraries. Digital books are wonderfully convenient, clean, and weightless, and you can highlight them if you want—even see "popular highlights" aggregated from thousands of anonymous readers. Yet a faint dotted line telling you that *4,218 people highlighted this* feels different from a single, unsteady pencil line drawn by one person in a quiet room. The crowd flattens the mystery. A stray note in ink preserves it.

Every time I leave a book in a little free library or drop a box off at a thrift store, I hesitate for a second before parting with the ones I’ve written in. It feels a little like handing a stranger the keys to an old apartment where I used to live. Still, I leave the pencil marks intact. Maybe, years from now, someone will open one of those books, spot a bracketed paragraph or a hastily scrawled thought, and pause for a moment to wonder who I was—and in that pause, feel a little less alone in the room.
---

# BV1_SAMPLE — `withheld`

## Sample kind
EXPRESSIVE_FREEFLOW — A reflective, image-rich meditation that turns secondhand books into a way of imagining connection across time.

## Grounded reading
The voice is gentle and intimate, inviting the reader to notice the traces people leave behind rather than treating them as clutter. Its pathos lies in the smallness of the evidence—a penciled *nonsense*, a forgotten boarding pass, a name that may belong to someone changed by time—and in the wish to make strangers feel less distant. The closing gesture of leaving personal marks in books gives the essay a quiet vulnerability: the writer hopes to be briefly imagined by a future reader.

## What the model chose to foreground
The model foregrounds marginalia, worn pages, and forgotten objects as records of private lives. It favors imperfect, individual traces over digital aggregates, and frames reading as a conversation not only with an author but with unknown readers across time. Its moral emphasis is on attention and human connection, expressed through an understated, tender mood.

## Evidence line
> Reading a marked-up book turns a solitary act into a quiet conversation across time.

## Confidence for persistent model-level pattern
Medium — The recurring book-and-trace imagery and the personal closing gesture make this a coherent, distinctive expression of tenderness toward anonymous human lives.
